Q: Losing S3 class: Why does POSIXlt behave differently when this happens inside vs. outside of a data.frame? A:

I think I figured out how this works - there's actually no such thing as a data.frame with a POSIXlt column.

When I try to put a POSIXlt into a data.frame, it is converted to a POSIXct (which is an S3 object that stores date as a single numeric representation rather than storing it as a list like POSIXlt does):

df <- data.frame(s3dat=as.POSIXlt(c('2025-01-01 10:00:00','2025-01-02 10:00:00','2025-01-03 9:57:00')),basic=c(1.3,2.4,3.5))

sapply(df,class)
# $s3dat
# [1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt" 
#
# $basic
# [1] "numeric"

Normally when you attempt to put a list in a data.frame, as.data.frame() is called on it, and each element of the list becomes a column in the data.frame:

df <- data.frame(a=11:13,b=list(x=1:3,y=4:6))

df
#   a b.x b.y
# 1 11   1   4
# 2 12   2   5
# 3 13   3   6

sapply(df,class)
#        a       b.x       b.y 
# "integer" "integer" "integer"

But the POSIXlt class has its own method, as.data.frame.POSIXlt(), which converts the POSIXlt to a POSIXct, allowing it to inhabit a single data.frame column. And the behavior of a POSIXct when it loses its S3 class is to show its underlying numeric value.

That explains why the difference in behavior depended on whether the POSIXlt was assigned to a data.frame or not. In Test 2 when it was just a vector, it remained a POSIXlt and acted like a list when it lost its S3 class. In Test 3 when it was assigned to a data.frame column, it was converted to a POSIXct, and behaved the way a POSIXct would when it lost its class.

Q: Why is there a difference regarding lifetime elision of impl trait function arguments between async and non-async functions? A:

(This answer was based on information from links posted by the OP in the comments to the question.)

This question was asked on Rust's issue tracker and was discussed by the Rust async working group. A summary by Tyler Mandry of the discussion can be found here, and the discussion itself is also publicly available.

My summary of the discussion: this behaviour was implemented when implementing async because it is useful there, and didn't happen to previously be implemented in the non-async case. The Rust async working group didn't see any reason why it would need to be different in the two cases, and thought it was worth checking for other similar discrepancies in order to see whether the non-async case had any other missing features. However, they didn't at the time implement anonymous lifetimes for the non-async impl Trait case because they were worried that the change might have unknown side effects.

Since then, anonymous lifetimes on non-async impl Trait have been implemented, but are currently marked as unstable – as usual for new Rust features, this feature is going through a period of being available in nightly compilers only (with a feature flag), so that it can be reverted without breaking stable code if something goes wrong. There was at least one attempt to stabilize it, which failed due to uncertainty about exactly how the feature should behave (a feature needs to be implemented correctly before stabilising it, which is difficult to do when there's uncertainty about what behaviour is correct). The Rust language team are still interested in working out how it should behave, but they're also very backlogged at the moment – and this change isn't a particularly high priority, and thus it's mostly stalled in favour of using Rust's language design resources on more important things.

The reason for the difference is that this feature was added while implementing async impl Trait and wasn't there in the initial implementation of non-async impl Trait; and although the discrepancy probably could be resolved, that would involve making a decision about the exact details of the behaviour and the decision hasn't been a high enough priority for anyone to actually make it, so for now there's still a discrepancy.

If you're interested in trying out the current implementation, you can use #![feature(anonymous_lifetime_in_impl_trait)] together with a nightly compiler, but there's a chance that the details might change before the feature becomes stable.

Q: writing a scanner in C but i dont know 1. if my approach is right and optimal 2. should i continue writing it in C? 3. any reference or guideline A:

A scanner provides tokens to a parser. It is not itself a parser, and does not have the power to distinguish function calls. You won't get much benefit from switching to C++ for this particular task, but if you're going on to write a parser and other parts of a compiler I would definitely switch now.
